title: ‘Cale88 Foods named after VP spouse, dentist’
summary: Cale88 Foods Corp., the banana chips exporter co-owned by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio and her dentist Lourdes Lebosada, takes its name from the first two letters of…
byline: Daphne Galvez, Bella Cariaso, Neil Jayson Servallos

blocks.text: November 21, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Cale88 Foods Corp., the banana chips exporter co-owned by Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband Manases Carpio and her dentist Lourdes Lebosada, takes its name from the first two letters of their surnames paired with a number symbolizing infinity, a trade official confirmed to the Senate impeachment court on Friday.

Testifying as a defense witness, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified the origin and pronunciation of the company’s name after presiding officer Francis Escudero asked whether it is pronounced with two syllables.
“When we asked the Davao BOI extension office, they said that in the ‘kah-leh’ the CA was the surname (of Carpio) while the LE was Lebosada, so ‘kah-leh,’” Rodolfo told the court.
“For Cale88, the eight was for infinity, so Cale88,” he added, referring to the number traditionally regarded as lucky.
“So, Cale88 was the pronunciation. So, at least we’re pronouncing it correctly,” Escudero replied.
Carpio and Lebosada each hold a 47.5 percent stake in Cale88, which is listed as a business interest of the Vice President’s husband.

The firm has drawn scrutiny during Duterte’s impeachment trial after Sen. Risa Hontiveros flagged its foreign remittances – including funds from Chinese entities and a Ukrainian company facing criminal complaints for money laundering and fraud.

Financial forensic expert Alexander Cabrera also previously testified that Cale88’s financial statements lacked reported accounts receivable, accounts payable and raw material inventory, despite substantial cash inflows and outflows.

The Anti-Money Laundering Council had earlier reported that the firm grossed more than P1 billion at one point and it received P776 million in foreign remittances from 2022 to 2025, including P319 million from China.
Zero employees
Rodolfo confirmed that Cale88 Foods Corp. had no employees in 2024 and only two employees in 2025.
The vice chairman and managing head of the Board of Investments made the confirmation during the cross-examination of counsel for the prosecution Erwin Matib.

Rodolfo was confronted with the general information sheet submitted by Cale88 to the BOI. Based on the document, Rodolfo said Cale88 reported three officers, zero rank-and-file employees and zero manpower complement in 2024.

Meanwhile, for 2025, the firm had two officers, two employees and no manpower complement. Rodolfo said he did not see any submission by Cale88 on its employees’ Social Security System and PhilHealth benefits.
FDA registration
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a certificate of product registration to Calle88 Food Corp. for sweetened banana chips on Aug. 17, 2022, valid until Aug. 16, 2027.

Defense counsel Justin Nicol Gular presented FDA Center for Food Regulation and Research director Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan to prove Calle88 was in the lawful legitimate export business of sweetened banana chips and had the requisite license to operate and certificate of product registration.
Pagayunan said the FDA initially rejected the application of Calle88.

“This was the packaging that was submitted in the initial application and it was evaluated in accordance to the regulations of the FDA on food labeling. That’s why there was a denial as a result of that initial evaluation,” she said.
Labor complaint
Cale88 may face a separate labor complaint after company records suggested its workers earned only about P75 a day, the House prosecution panel said.
Panel spokesman Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong questioned payroll figures submitted to BOI showing that Cale88 had 115 workers but spent only P3.112 million on their annual compensation.

Based on those figures, he said each worker would have received an average of P27,061 a year, or about P2,255 a month, assuming the payroll was divided equally among employees working throughout the year.
